_doc: Predicate head -> the English words that mean it, for translation.
Distinct from a pack's `predicate_words`, which is that language's own
REALIZATION of a head. English realizes `precedes` as 'comes before' and
that is the right English; but 'comes before' is a poor thing to hand to a
dictionary, which keys on 'precede'. This table is the translation source,
so it gives the CITATION form and the plainest phrasing, not the idiom.
Why it is needed at all: a head like `implies` is an inflected English verb
and `sub` is an abbreviation. Neither is a dictionary key in any language,
so 400+ derived grammars were printing the head itself -- `left_of`, an
internal identifier with an underscore in it, straight onto the page.
A grammar with its own hand-written entry never consults this. It is the
fallback that lets a derived grammar compose something in the right
language, token by token, instead of leaking the key.
The set is closed and small on purpose. A coined nonce word must pass
through untouched -- most of what this curriculum names is invented per
episode, and translating it would destroy the lesson -- so only heads
listed here are ever spelled out.
The comparison relations (gt, lt, eq, ne, ge, le) are here for the same
reason: they are abbreviations, not words, and every derived grammar was
printing 'gt' where a language's own comparative belongs. A pack with its
own idiomatic entry -- English 'is greater than' -- still wins; this is
only what a grammar falls back to.
